correctness.rationale: Every m-plane is the common kernel and image of exactly |GL_m| possible factors. Nontransverse kernels give a nonzero common annihilated vector; for complementary kernels the two restrictions are independent uniform isomorphisms A,B and C=diag(AB,-BA). Complements are graphs of q^(m^2) maps; AB is uniform and BA conjugate to it. The signed direct sum is cyclic exactly when T is cyclic and its opposite characteristic polynomial is coprime to its own. In characteristic two the doubled module is never cyclic. For odd q, the primary centralizer of a single phi^k block has q^(d(k-1))(q^d-1) units, giving the local orbit factors and formal coefficient law. An independent analytic simplification avoids the full cycle index: multiply H by the polynomial zeta product over phi!=t of [1-(z/q)^deg(phi)] = (1-z)/(1-z/q). This yields (1-z)H as (1-z/q) times the paired factors with [1-(z/q)^d]^2 and the self-opposite factors [1-(z/q)^d]. The paired factors have first-order residual coefficient 2/[q^d(q^d-1)] in z^d and quadratic remainder O((|z|/q)^(2d)); self-opposites are g(t^2) with count at most q^(d/2). Normal convergence on every closed disk of radius smaller than sqrt(q) gives the exponential coefficient tail. At z=1 the normalized paired factors are 1+q^(-2d). Writing A,B for the paired and self-opposite half-degree Euler products, even-polynomial factorization gives AB=Z=(1-v)/(1-qv); irreducible g(t^2) is equivalent to the norm of a root of g being nonsquare. The quadratic-character Euler product is 1 because each positive degree has equal signed constant-term counts; its nonsquare factors give B(v)^2/B(v^2)=Z(v). Thus A(v)/(A(v^2)B(v))=1/Z(v^2). At v=q^-2 this gives the stated kappa after the prefactor 1-q^-1; the Gaussian-binomial complement fraction tends to Phi_q. Independent bounded GF(9) enumeration (arithmetic in F_3[i]/(i^2+1)) gave 5104/5760=319/360 at m=2, using the equivalent invertible 2x2 test of nonscalar and nonzero trace. Inspected the frozen checker and recorded output, not executing it; its finite prime-field tests do not prove the asymptotic or the extension-field result.
